subject: Estimating correlations between lower parameters... problematic

messages.author: cf47bbe63da1f3ae
messages.subject: Estimating correlations between lower parameters... problematic
parts:
I have a hierarchical multivariate time series model - something roughly like:

parameters{
vector[15] hypermeans;
vector[15] hypersd;
vector[(15*15-15)/2] hypercorr;
vector[15] subjectparams [nsubjects];
}
transformed parameters{
//create cholesky factor from transformations of hypercorr and hypersd
//create subject specific time series matrices from subject params and cholesky covariance and transformed hypermeans
}
model{
//sample all parameters as standard normal
//increment log prob using kalman filter for subject level likelihoods
}

this works very well when I fix the correlations of the cholesky factor matrix to 0, but when I try to also estimate the correlation between parameters, the treedepth gets much deeper or (if at max treedepth) I get very slow moving chains. I've tried both centered and non centered parameterisations, tighter priors on the correlations (also tried the standard lkj approach). The model has gotten a bit complex so I doubt anyone wants to diagnose it, but I've verified it's behaviour with simulated data and printing the matrices at various points...  I just wonder if anyone has insight as to whether this massive increase in complexity is expected, when the correlations between parameters are included, and maybe suggestions for other things to try?

messages.author: da33143a8db60ce8
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Estimating correlations between population level parameters... problematic
parts:
In my experience, this sort of model works best if you parameterize so that, a priori, you'd expect close to 0 correlations between parameters.  Then you can get away with setting corrs to be 0, or putting a fairly strong prior on the corr matrix that is centered at the identity matrix.  It's hard to say more without knowing the example, but I'm guessing you can do some reparameterization of your 15 parameters.
A

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Estimating correlations between population level parameters... problematic
parts:
You can think of setting them to single values as being
an approximate Bayesian technique. Fixing hyperparameters
tends to underestimate posterior uncertainty compared to
estimating them along with other parameters. In estimating
then fixing the hyperparameters, this is related to empirical
Bayes (another approximate Bayesian inference technique, often
carried out with max marginal likelihood).

- Bob

parts:
Sure, it's not the most straightforward process I guess! But yes it ends up back in the density because I normalise the subject parameters according to the computed cholesky factor (which is a mixture of sampled hypersd's, and hypercorrelations computed from sampled subject parameters), and use the normalised params for density calcs. Something like:

parameters{
vector[npars] hypermeans;
vector[npars] hypersd;
vector[npars] subjectparams [nsubjects];
}
transformed parameters{
vector[(npars*npars-npars)/2] hypercorr;
vector[npars*nsubjects] normalisedsubjectparams;
//calculate correlations from subjectparams, use these along with sampled hypersd to generate inverse of cholesky factor of subjectparams covariance
//normalise using inverse cholesky and vectorise subjectparams into normalisedsubjectparams
//create subject specific time series matrices from transformations of subject params and hypermeans
}
model{
//'sample' hypermeans, hypersds and normalisedsubjectparams as standard normal
//perhaps 'sample' hypercorrs according to desired prior - not necessary and I'm not certain if appropriate given transformations
//increment log prob with inverse cholesky factor of subjectparams covariance
//increment log prob using kalman filter for subject level time series likelihoods

}


On Saturday, July 23, 2016 at 9:37:14 PM UTC+2, Bob Carpenter wrote:
That is indeed what I thought.  I'm not sure
how what you're suggesting would work in Stan.  Unless
it feeds back into the density, it won't affect
sampling.

- Bob


On Jul 23, 2016, at 3:30 PM, Charles Driver <cdriv...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Thanks Bob - I'm not sure if we're 100% clear though, when I say fixing them, they are being fixed to different values (based on the sampled lower level parameters) at every iteration. Was that how you interpreted me? Your last sentence makes it sound like you think I'm doing some sort of two pass approach.
>
> On Saturday, July 23, 2016 at 9:19:45 PM UTC+2, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> You can think of setting them to single values as being
> an approximate Bayesian technique.  Fixing hyperparameters
> tends to underestimate posterior uncertainty compared to
> estimating them along with other parameters.  In estimating
> then fixing the hyperparameters, this is related to empirical
> Bayes (another approximate Bayesian inference technique, often
> carried out with max marginal likelihood).
>
> - Bob
>
> > On Jul 21, 2016, at 2:44 PM, Charles Driver <cdriv...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >
> > Well, instead of sampling the hyper correlations I am now setting them deterministically based on the correlation of the sampled lower level parameters...  this is working great from a computational / empirical perspective, have you seen such an approach or have any thoughts on how one might justify it? I would be unsure about the relation between the posterior of the determined correlations and the 'true / sampled correlation' posterior, so wouldn't lean on the correlations for inferential purposes, but other than that I would expect things to be 'fine'...
> >
> > On Monday, July 18, 2016 at 11:07:59 PM UTC+2, Charles Driver wrote:
> > I guess that would be one way out, seems a little ugly but maybe not more so in reality than the other model decisions...
> >
> > On Monday, July 18, 2016 at 10:56:14 PM UTC+2, Andrew Gelman wrote:
> > Hi, yes, I see what you're saying.   You could try setting most of the corrs to 0 and just estimate a few of them?
> >> On Jul 18, 2016, at 4:51 PM, Charles Driver <cdriv...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >>
> >> Thanks, I have done my best to parameterise in such a way as to remove correlations that would be implied by the model, but I can't see how one could account for correlations given only by the particular data? consider that two of the parameters are the intercepts for processes 1 and 2 -- for some problems, subjects that tend to be high on process 1 may tend to also be high on process two, while for other problems this may not be the case.
> >>
> >> On Monday, July 18, 2016 at 10:38:22 PM UTC+2, Andrew Gelman wrote:
> >> In my experience, this sort of model works best if you parameterize so that, a priori, you'd expect close to 0 correlations between parameters.  Then you can get away with setting corrs to be 0, or putting a fairly strong prior on the corr matrix that is centered at the identity matrix.  It's hard to say more without knowing the example, but I'm guessing you can do some reparameterization of your 15 parameters.
> >> A
> >>
> >>> On Jul 18, 2016, at 4:08 PM, Charles Driver <cdriv...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >>>
> >>> I have a hierarchical multivariate time series model - something roughly like:
> >>>
> >>> parameters{
> >>> vector[15] hypermeans;
> >>> vector[15] hypersd;
> >>> vector[(15*15-15)/2] hypercorr;
> >>> vector[15] subjectparams [nsubjects];
> >>> }
> >>> transformed parameters{
> >>> //create cholesky factor from transformations of hypercorr and hypersd
> >>> //create non centered subject specific time series matrices from subject params and cholesky covariance and transformed hypermeans
> >>> }
> >>> model{
> >>> //sample all parameters as standard normal
> >>> //increment log prob using kalman filter for subject level likelihoods
> >>> }
> >>>
> >>> this works very well when I fix the correlations of the cholesky factor matrix to 0, but when I try to also estimate the correlation between parameters, the treedepth gets much deeper or (if at max treedepth) I get very slow moving chains. I've tried both centered and non centered parameterisations, tighter priors on the correlations (also tried the standard lkj approach). The model has gotten a bit complex so I doubt anyone wants to diagnose it, but I've verified it's behaviour with simulated data and printing the matrices at various points...  I just wonder if anyone has insight as to whether this massive increase in complexity is expected, when the correlations between parameters are included, and maybe suggestions for other things to try?
